q: Nigeria became independent on
e: Nigeria gained independence on 1 October 1960.

q: Who heads the judiciary at the federal level in Nigeria?
e: The Chief Justice of Nigeria heads the judiciary.

q: The theory of separation of powers is associated with
e: Montesquieu proposed separating legislative, executive and judicial powers.

q: A system that shares power between central and regional governments is
e: Federalism divides power between central and regional governments.

q: The main function of the legislature is to
e: The legislature makes laws.

q: ECOWAS was formed in
e: ECOWAS was founded in 1975 through the Treaty of Lagos.

q: The first Executive President of Nigeria was
e: Shehu Shagari became Executive President in 1979.

q: The federal legislature of Nigeria is called the
e: The National Assembly (Senate plus House of Representatives) is the federal legislature.

q: Government by the people is
e: Democracy means rule by the people.

q: The right of citizens to vote is called
e: Suffrage is the right to vote.

q: The organ of government that interprets laws is the
e: The judiciary interprets laws in the courts.

q: Nigeria's present constitution came into effect in

q: Nigeria's first Prime Minister was
e: Sir Abubakar Tafawa Balewa led the government at independence.

q: The first President of Nigeria was
e: Nnamdi Azikiwe became the first President when Nigeria became a republic.

q: Nigeria became a republic in
e: Nigeria became a republic on 1 October 1963.

q: The Northern and Southern Protectorates were amalgamated in
e: Lord Lugard amalgamated them in 1914.

q: Indirect rule in Nigeria is associated with
e: Lord Lugard used traditional rulers to govern for the British.

q: The seat of government officially moved from Lagos to Abuja in
e: The move took place in December 1991.

q: How many states does Nigeria have (not counting the FCT)?
e: Nigeria has 36 states plus the Federal Capital Territory.

q: How many local government areas does Nigeria have?
e: Nigeria has 774 local government areas.

q: The legislature at the federal level in Nigeria is the
e: The National Assembly is made up of the Senate and the House of Representatives.

q: How many senators does Nigeria have?
e: Three per state (36 × 3 = 108) plus one for the FCT makes 109.

q: How many members are in the House of Representatives?
e: The House of Representatives has 360 members.

q: The organ of government that interprets the law is the
e: The judiciary (the courts) interprets and applies the law.

q: The organ of government that makes laws is the
e: The legislature makes laws.

q: The body that conducts elections in Nigeria is
e: INEC is the Independent National Electoral Commission.

q: EFCC stands for
e: EFCC is the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission.

q: ECOWAS was established in
e: ECOWAS was formed by the Treaty of Lagos in 1975.

q: The headquarters of the African Union is in
e: The African Union is headquartered in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia.

q: The headquarters of OPEC is in
e: OPEC has its headquarters in Vienna, Austria.

q: The United Nations was founded in
e: The UN was founded in 1945.

q: Universal adult suffrage means
o: all qualified adults have the right to vote
e: Every qualified adult citizen has the right to vote.

q: A political system in which only one party is allowed to rule is a
e: This is a one-party system.

q: A bill becomes law after
e: After passing the legislature, a bill needs presidential assent.

q: The rule of law means that
o: only the poor obey the law
everyone, including leaders, is subject to the law
e: No one is above the law.

q: A state headed by a hereditary ruler is a
e: A monarchy is headed by a king or queen who inherits the position.

q: In a unitary system, power is
e: Unitary governments keep power at the centre.

q: Fundamental human rights are contained in which chapter of the 1999 Constitution?
e: Chapter IV covers fundamental rights.

q: The first military coup in Nigeria took place in
e: The first coup happened in January 1966.

q: The Nigerian Civil War was fought between
e: The civil war lasted from 1967 to 1970.

q: The supreme and ultimate power of a state to make and enforce laws within its territory is known as
e: Sovereignty is the supreme, independent power of a state over its territory and people.

q: Power that is generally accepted by the people as rightful is described as
e: Authority is legitimate power, accepted by those over whom it is exercised.

q: A constitution that is difficult to amend because of a special procedure is said to be
e: A rigid constitution requires a special, usually demanding, amendment procedure.

q: Which of the following countries is a well-known example of one with an unwritten constitution?
e: Britain's constitution is not contained in a single written document.

q: The fusion of the executive and legislative branches is a feature of a
e: In a parliamentary system, ministers are also members of the legislature.

q: Senate confirmation of ministerial nominees made by the President is an example of
e: It shows the legislature checking the executive's appointment power.

q: An electoral system in which parties win seats in proportion to the votes they receive is
e: Proportional representation allocates seats according to each party's share of votes.

q: Which of the following is an example of a pressure group in Nigeria?
e: The NLC seeks to influence government policy without seeking to govern, unlike a political party.

q: A by-election is held when
o: a seat in the legislature becomes vacant between general elections
the results of an election are cancelled nationwide
e: By-elections fill vacancies that occur between general elections.

q: In a federation such as Nigeria, powers not assigned to the central government are called
e: Residual powers are those not listed for the centre and are left to the component units.

q: The Clifford Constitution of 1922 introduced the elective principle in
e: Elections to the Legislative Council were held in Lagos and Calabar.

q: The Richards Constitution of 1946 divided Nigeria into
e: It created the Northern, Western and Eastern regions.

q: The constitution that formally introduced a federal structure in Nigeria was the
e: The 1954 Lyttelton Constitution established Nigeria as a federation.

q: The Nigerian National Democratic Party, formed in 1923, was founded by
e: Herbert Macaulay founded the NNDP, the first Nigerian political party, after the Clifford Constitution.

q: The National Council of Nigeria and the Cameroons (NCNC) was formed in
e: The NCNC was formed in 1944 with Herbert Macaulay as president and Nnamdi Azikiwe as secretary.

q: The warrant chief system was a feature of British colonial rule in
e: The British appointed warrant chiefs in Igbo areas that lacked centralised chiefs.

q: The Sokoto Caliphate was established in the early nineteenth century by
e: Usman dan Fodio led the Fulani jihad that began in 1804 and founded the Caliphate.

q: In the pre-colonial Oyo Empire, the council that checked the powers of the Alaafin was the
e: The Oyomesi, headed by the Bashorun, could check the Alaafin.

q: Nigeria's 12 states were created in 1967 by the government of
e: General Yakubu Gowon created twelve states in May 1967.

q: The 1976 Local Government Reform made local government a
e: The reform established local government as the third tier of government.

q: The Fundamental Objectives and Directive Principles of State Policy are contained in which chapter of the 1999 Constitution?
e: Chapter II contains the Fundamental Objectives and Directive Principles of State Policy.

q: The Organisation of African Unity (OAU) was founded in
e: The OAU was founded in Addis Ababa in 1963.

q: The African Union replaced the Organisation of African Unity in
e: The AU was launched in 2002 as successor to the OAU.

q: The Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) was formed in
e: OPEC was founded in Baghdad in 1960; Nigeria joined later, in 1971.

q: Nigeria became a member of the Commonwealth of Nations in
e: Nigeria joined the Commonwealth at independence in 1960.

q: The first Governor-General of Nigeria after the 1914 amalgamation was
e: Lord Lugard became Governor-General of the amalgamated Nigeria in 1914.

q: The presidential system adopted in Nigeria's 1979 Constitution was modelled on that of the
e: The 1979 Constitution copied the American presidential system.

q: One major function of political parties is to
o: aggregate the interests of citizens and contest elections
e: Parties bring together interests and seek power by contesting elections.

q: Government by a small privileged group is called
e: Oligarchy means rule by a few people.

q: The process through which a foreigner legally becomes a citizen of a country is
e: Naturalisation grants citizenship to a foreigner who meets legal requirements.
